paragraphs.source_en: The transition from the Epipalaeolithic to the Mesolithic phase was gradual, without any break in the material culture. Before the Mesolithic period the Epipalaeolithic occupation lasted for more than one thousand years, with the same shelters being frequented. Therefore, the question is this: why would the hunter-gatherers start to make paintings from 8,800 BP and not earlier? What impulse would have caused a sudden rise in the artistic production, during an apparently continuous cultural phase? It is possible that the progressive deterioration of the humid climate and the modification in the subsistence strategies, with an increasing exploitation of the vegetal resources in the Mesolithic, provoked a change in the minds of hunter-gatherers which would have ignited an artistic tradition.

paragraphs.source_en: However, there is no doubt that before the Mesolithic period people were aware of the qualities of red ochre and other pigments and how they interacted with the rock surface. The archaeological record testifies that the Epipalaeolithic hunters were a complex society with excellent quality lithics made often from "exotic" raw materials found only outside the area with the Round Head paintings. Their notion of "art" is further witnessed with the existence of ostrich beads. Although the humid conditions in which they lived may have destroyed possible coloured organic material, there is no reason for which these developed and organised groups should completely ignore any painting activity. If the hypothesis of the Epipalaeolithic origin of the Round Head art is correct, how and why did it start?

paragraphs.source_en: The onset of the wetter climate in the lowlands in the 10th millennium BP represented an important change in the Central Saharan environment. Before this date the mountains were isolated because they were surrounded by vast dry plains which would have impeded people and animals in reaching this area. With favourable conditions corresponding with the Epipalaeolithic phase, new subsistence strategies developed. Based on the lithic industry and settlement Aumassip (2004) argues that the Epipalaeolithic represents a rupture in the prehistoric times throughout the whole of the Sahara; the sites became much more numerous and true homesteads are recognisable. The grinding equipment and pottery testify to this general change and attest to a transformation in alimentation, heralding the Neolithic phase.
